ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Addiction Medicine Referral — Elvis Presley

code.originalText: Establishing primary care for fatigue, weight gain, constipation, daytime sleepiness and high blood pressure, with many prescribed drugs from several prescribers: a full medication reconciliation and prescription drug monitoring program review, a nonjudgmental substance use assessment, safety, and an addiction medicine referral

text.paragraph: Long-term prescription opioids and benzodiazepines from five prescribers, with fatigue, weight gain, constipation, daytime sleepiness and high blood pressure, in a 39-year-old touring singer who wants to change how he takes his medicines. Please assess for substance use disorders and advise on medication for opioid use disorder and a safe benzodiazepine plan. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the day of his one-week primary care review, at his request before a Las Vegas engagement in five weeks. [S]

list.item: Does he meet DSM-5-TR criteria for opioid and sedative use disorders, and how severe?
Should he start buprenorphine, and how: in the office or at home, standard or low-dose start?
How should the two benzodiazepines be managed alongside buprenorphine, and at what taper pace?
What monitoring do you advise (urine testing, monitoring program, visit frequency, naloxone)?
How should care be planned around a Las Vegas engagement and a tour this autumn?

text.paragraph: Opioids for about five years for back and neck pain from performing, and sedatives for sleep after shows. A hospital stay some years ago in which he was withdrawn from opioids. The monitoring program shows five prescribers and three pharmacies in the past year: hydromorphone 4 mg about five a day and oxycodone 10 mg with acetaminophen about three a day (about 145 MME), diazepam 10 mg three times daily, alprazolam 1 mg up to three a day, and phentermine 37.5 mg each morning (stopped today because of hypertension and glaucoma), with a nonprescription diphenhydramine sleep aid (also stopped). He takes more than prescribed, has tried to cut down, and has cravings; he has never injected and uses no illicit drugs or alcohol (AUDIT-C 0; DAST-10 7). PHQ-9 8 and GAD-7 9, item 9 scored 0; no suicidal thoughts; structured safety assessment done, firearms to be locked. Blood pressure 154/98, pulse 94; BMI 32.5; ALT 72, AST 52, GGT 78; hemoglobin A1c 5.8%; ECG normal, QTc 436 ms. STOP-Bang 6, Epworth 14; in-laboratory polysomnography booked. Glaucoma on latanoprost. Today: naloxone, a single-prescriber agreement, seven-day supplies of his current opioids and benzodiazepines at the verified doses, a locked box and take-back; he preferred to discuss buprenorphine with the specialist before starting [S]

list.item: He is tired all the time, sleepy in the afternoon and cannot keep up the energy his shows need. [S]
He has put on weight and feels bloated and constipated, and is self-conscious about it on stage. [S]
He wants to stop needing so many pills without going through withdrawal or missing a show. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Elvis Aron Presley was born in a two-room house in Tupelo, Mississippi, on January 8, 1935; his family moved to Memphis when he was 13. [D]

He made his first record in 1953, became a national star in 1956, served in the Army in West Germany from 1958 to 1960, and by the 1970s performed long engagements in Las Vegas and toured constantly. In 1974 he played Las Vegas from January 26 to February 9, toured through much of March, including four shows in Memphis on March 16 and 17 and a recorded show there on March 20, played Lake Tahoe from May 16 to 26, toured again in mid-June, and took a few weeks off at Graceland from early July. [D]

From October 15 to November 1, 1973, he was treated at Baptist Memorial Hospital in Memphis under an assumed name; at the 1981 trial of his physician, an internal medicine specialist who reviewed the records testified that the consulting physicians were "withdrawing him from narcotic drugs." [D]
He had glaucoma, including an episode of acute angle-closure glaucoma in 1971, and was under the care of one ophthalmologist from 1971 on. [D]
It was believed that he neither smoked nor drank alcohol. [D]

text.paragraph: 10 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

list.item: Singer and performer since his teens; long engagements in Las Vegas and multi-week concert tours with two shows on some nights; between tours he is at his home in Memphis. A three-week Las Vegas engagement begins in about six weeks and a tour after that [S]
Lives at his home in Memphis with household staff and friends who work for him and travel with him on tour [S]

Prescriptions from five prescribers filled at three pharmacies over the past year, by the prescription drug monitoring program; says he started opioids for back and neck pain from performing, and sedatives for sleep after shows; also a nonprescription diphenhydramine sleep aid most nights, stopped today because of his glaucoma and the sedatives; no pills from any source other than a prescription or a pharmacy shelf; never injected [S]
Alcohol: none (AUDIT-C 0). Tobacco: never [S]
Eats one large meal after shows late at night; snacks on the tour bus; little activity between tours apart from karate practice [S]
Keeps several firearms at home; agreed today to store them locked and unloaded, with ammunition separate, while the medicines are being changed [S]
Strengths: devotion to his audience and his music, his faith and gospel singing, loyalty to the people around him, and his own decision to change how he takes his medicines [S]

list.item: Fatigue, weight gain of about 14 kg in two years, constipation with a bowel movement every five to seven days, loud snoring with daytime sleepiness, and high blood pressure readings, in a man taking two opioids, two benzodiazepines and an appetite suppressant from five prescribers; under evaluation with addiction medicine, a sleep study and home blood pressure readings: active, confirmed [S]

Obesity, class 1 (BMI 32.5), with prediabetes (hemoglobin A1c 5.8%); recorded without stigma; weight gain began with long touring schedules, night eating after shows and an appetite suppressant that stopped working: active, confirmed [S]

Glaucoma secondary to steroids, both eyes, mild stage, after an acute angle-closure episode treated years ago; intraocular pressure controlled on latanoprost under his ophthalmologist; anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs to be avoided: active, confirmed [S]

Safe prescribing of controlled drugs: a brown-bag reconciliation of every medicine, a prescription drug monitoring program check before every controlled prescription, a written single-prescriber agreement with one pharmacy, urine drug testing explained as part of care, seven-day supplies at first, a locked box, and take-back of unused tablets; no controlled drug stopped abruptly. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022 (2022); Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (2025); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026) [S]

Overdose prevention: naloxone nasal spray at home and in the tour bag, two people around him taught to use it, no alcohol or other sedatives, and the danger of opioids with benzodiazepines and with the sleep apnea that is suspected explained. Guideline: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022 (2022); The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020) [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment, a written safety plan, firearms locked and unloaded with ammunition separate, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at each review. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension, glaucoma, and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Constipation on opioids: polyethylene glycol daily with senna as needed, fluids and fiber; a peripherally acting opioid antagonist only if these fail; an abdominal radiograph only for pain, distension or vomiting. Guideline: American Gastroenterological Association Institute Guideline on the Medical Management of Opioid-Induced Constipation (2019); American Gastroenterological Association-American College of Gastroenterology Clinical Practice Guideline: Pharmacological Management of Chronic Idiopathic Constipation (2023) [S]

Glaucoma: latanoprost continued, his ophthalmologist kept informed of every new medicine, no phentermine, decongestant or anticholinergic sleep aid, steroids only when essential and with his ophthalmologist's knowledge, and urgent care for eye pain with halos. Guideline: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma Preferred Practice Pattern (2020); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypertension, glaucoma, and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Performing and touring: no medication change in the week before an engagement, weekly video visits while away, controlled prescriptions sent only to one named pharmacy, a written plan for missed doses, naloxone and any prescribed devices in the tour bag, and a letter he controls for venues. Guideline: The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020); Joint Clinical Practice Guideline on Benzodiazepine Tapering: Considerations When Risks Outweigh Benefits (2025) [S]
